claim: p53 is the most mutated protein in cancer cells with more than 2000 different mutations identified so far.
source: The tumour suppressor p53 is the most mutated protein in cancer cells with more than 2000 different mutations identified so far (Joerger et al., 2006; Funk et al., 2025).
evidence: Supported by citations to Joerger et al., 2006 and Funk et al., 2025

claim: In tumour cells with wild-type p53, its activity is inhibited by the overexpression of E3 ligases such as Mdm2.
source: In tumour cells with wild-type p53, its activity is also inhibited for example by the overexpression of E3 ligases such as Mdm2 (Haupt et al., 1997; Kubbutat et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Haupt et al., 1997 and Kubbutat et al., 1997

claim: p53 structurally consists of a central DNA-binding domain (DBD), an N-terminal transactivation domain (TAD) and a C-terminal oligomerization domain (OD) through which it forms tetramers.
source: Structurally, it consists of a central DNA-binding domain (DBD), an N-terminal transactivation domain (TAD) and a C-terminal oligomerization domain (OD) through which it forms tetramers (Joerger and Fersht, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Joerger and Fersht, 2007

claim: Mutations in p53 mainly cluster in the DBD.
source: Mutations can occur in all these domains but mainly cluster in the DBD (Joerger et al., 2006; Funk et al., 2025).
evidence: Supported by citations to Joerger et al., 2006 and Funk et al., 2025

claim: High-affinity DNA binding requires the formation of tetramers.
source: High-affinity DNA binding requires the formation of tetramers which enables dominant negative effects of cancer mutations in the DBD as mutant p53 and wild-type p53 can form mixed tetramers via their ODs with strongly reduced binding affinity.
evidence: Stated as a fact in the manuscript text

claim: Mutant p53 and wild-type p53 can form mixed tetramers via their ODs with strongly reduced binding affinity.
source: High-affinity DNA binding requires the formation of tetramers which enables dominant negative effects of cancer mutations in the DBD as mutant p53 and wild-type p53 can form mixed tetramers via their ODs with strongly reduced binding affinity.
evidence: Stated as a fact in the manuscript text

claim: Mutations in the DBD of p63 result in developmental defects based on a dominant negative mechanism.
source: Similar dominant negative effects are known from the p53 family member p63 in which mutations in the DBD result in developmental defects based on a dominant negative mechanism (Osterburg et al., 2023; Celli et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Osterburg et al., 2023 and Celli et al., 1999

claim: p63 and p73 exist in multiple different isoforms that are created by the combination of different promoters with splicing events in the C-terminus.
source: The discovery of p63 and the third family member p73 has revealed that these two proteins exist in multiple different isoforms that are created by the combination of different promoters with splicing events in the C-terminus which strongly influences the transcriptional activity of these isoforms (Osterburg and Dötsch, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Osterburg and Dötsch, 2022

claim: Different isoforms have been identified for p53.
source: Different isoforms have also been identified for p53 (Bourdon et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citation to Bourdon et al., 2005

claim: p53 isoforms are responsible for increased cancer metastasis.
source: it has been proposed that these isoforms are responsible for increased cancer metastasis as well as premature aging upon dysregulation.
evidence: Stated as a proposal in the literature

claim: p63 and p73 isoforms do not contain truncations in folded domains.
source: In contrast to the p63 and p73 isoforms, which do not contain truncations in folded domains, most of the isoforms of p53 contain only parts of either the DBD or the OD.
evidence: Stated as a fact in the manuscript text

claim: Most of the isoforms of p53 contain only parts of either the DBD or the OD.
source: In contrast to the p63 and p73 isoforms, which do not contain truncations in folded domains, most of the isoforms of p53 contain only parts of either the DBD or the OD.
evidence: Stated as a fact in the manuscript text

claim: A deletion of the OD prevents the formation of tetramers which are required for high-affinity DNA binding.
source: A deletion of the OD not only prevents the formation of tetramers which are required for high-affinity DNA binding, it also deletes the nuclear export signal, thereby influencing the subcellular localization of these isoforms.
evidence: Stated as a fact in the manuscript text

claim: A deletion of the OD deletes the nuclear export signal, thereby influencing the subcellular localization of p53 isoforms.
source: A deletion of the OD not only prevents the formation of tetramers which are required for high-affinity DNA binding, it also deletes the nuclear export signal, thereby influencing the subcellular localization of these isoforms.
evidence: Stated as a fact in the manuscript text

claim: The wild-type p53 DBD is only metastable with a melting temperature of ~43°C.
source: The wild-type p53 DBD is known to be only metastable with a melting temperature of ~43°C (Joerger et al., 2006; Bullock et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Joerger et al., 2006 and Bullock et al., 1997

claim: Many p53 mutations found in tumours destabilize the DBD further, resulting in unfolding and gain of function effects via co-aggregation with other cellular factors.
source: Many p53 mutations found in tumours destabilize the DBD further, resulting in unfolding and due to the exposure of aggregation-prone peptide sequences in gain of function effects via co-aggregation with other cellular factors (Xu et al., 2011; Levine et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Xu et al., 2011 and Levine et al., 1995

claim: The metastability of the p53 DBD, combined with the cooperative folding behaviour of single domain proteins, predicts that isoforms containing a truncated DBD cannot properly fold but have a high aggregation potential.
source: This metastability, combined with the in general cooperative folding behaviour of single domain proteins, strongly predicts that the isoforms containing a truncated DBD cannot properly fold but have a high aggregation potential, similar to mutant p53 with destabilizing mutations.
evidence: Based on logical inference from known properties of p53 DBD and protein folding principles

claim: Individual p53 isoforms have been assigned specific regulatory functions in different cellular systems.
source: p53 isoforms have been studied in different cellular systems and individual isoforms have been assigned specific regulatory functions (Zhang et al., 2019; Horikawa et al., 2014; Gadea et al., 2016; Roth et al., 2016; Fujita et al., 2009; Mondal et al., 2013; Turnquist et al., 2016; von Muhlinen et al., 2018; Gong et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: A comprehensive biochemical characterization of p53 isoforms is missing.
source: However, a comprehensive biochemical characterization of these isoforms is missing and we propose that many of the observed effects can be assigned to co-aggregation of these isoforms with wild-type p53 as well as other cellular factors such as the other members of the p53 protein family.
evidence: Stated as a gap in the literature

claim: Many of the observed effects of p53 isoforms can be assigned to co-aggregation with wild-type p53 as well as other cellular factors.
source: However, a comprehensive biochemical characterization of these isoforms is missing and we propose that many of the observed effects can be assigned to co-aggregation of these isoforms with wild-type p53 as well as other cellular factors such as the other members of the p53 protein family.
evidence: Stated as a proposal by the authors

claim: A total of 14 p53 isoforms with various truncations have been identified.
source: So far, a total of 14 p53 isoforms with various truncations have been identified.
evidence: Stated as a fact in the manuscript text

claim: Alternative translation start sites create the isoforms Δ40p53, Δ133p53, and Δ160p53.
source: Compared to the wild-type p53 form (from now on named wtp53) alternative translation start sites create the isoforms Δ40p53, Δ133p53, and Δ160p53, each lacking the indicated number of amino acids from the N-terminus (Joruiz and Bourdon, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Joruiz and Bourdon, 2016

claim: The Δ40p53 variants have a deletion of the first 40 amino acids of the N‐terminus including the transactivation domain 1 (TAD1).
source: The Δ40p53 variants have a deletion of the first 40 amino acids of the N‐terminus including the transactivation domain 1 (TAD1) (Krois et al., 2016) but contain a wild-type DBD and OD.
evidence: Supported by citation to Krois et al., 2016

claim: The Δ40p53 variants contain a wild-type DBD and OD.
source: The Δ40p53 variants have a deletion of the first 40 amino acids of the N‐terminus including the transactivation domain 1 (TAD1) (Krois et al., 2016) but contain a wild-type DBD and OD.
evidence: Stated as a fact in the manuscript text

claim: The Δ133p53 and Δ160p53 isoforms lack the complete TAD and parts of the DBD.
source: The Δ133p53 and Δ160p53 isoforms lack, in addition to the complete TAD, parts of the DBD.
evidence: Stated as a fact in the manuscript text

claim: Different N-terminal isoforms can be combined with three different C-termini called α, β, and γ.
source: These different N-terminal isoforms can be combined with three different C-termini called α, β, and γ.
evidence: Stated as a fact in the manuscript text

claim: Only the wild-type αC-terminus contains a full OD.
source: Only the wild-type αC-terminus contains a full OD, the β- and ɣC-termini have a truncated OD with isoform-specific extensions.
evidence: Stated as a fact in the manuscript text

claim: The β- and ɣC-termini have a truncated OD with isoform-specific extensions.
source: Only the wild-type αC-terminus contains a full OD, the β- and ɣC-termini have a truncated OD with isoform-specific extensions.
evidence: Stated as a fact in the manuscript text

claim: wtp53 showed a strong transcriptional activity in luciferase reporter assays.
source: wt-p53 showed a strong transcriptional activity (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-C

claim: The artificial construct TA-DBD-OD showed even higher transcriptional activity than wtp53.
source: An even higher activity was seen for the artificial construct TA-DBD-OD, lacking the CTD.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: The p53R175H mutant shows a complete loss of transcriptional activity.
source: As a negative control, we used the p53R175H mutant, which harbours a structural DBD mutation leading to a complete loss of transcriptional activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: TAp53β and TAp53γ showed a slight transactivation capacity, which is several-fold lower than the wtp53 activity.
source: TAp53β and TAp53γ still contain the full-length TA and DBD domains but lack the OD and therefore are unable to form tetramers. They showed a slight transactivation capacity, which is, however, several-fold lower than the wtp53 activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: No transactivation capacity was detected for TAΔp53α.
source: In agreement with a previous study (Chan and Poon, 2007), no transactivation capacity was detected for TAΔp53α which lacks part of its DBD and linker region to its OD as well as the nuclear localization signal (NLS) and for the p53ψ isoform (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and citation to Chan and Poon, 2007

claim: No transactivation capacity was detected for the p53ψ isoform.
source: In agreement with a previous study (Chan and Poon, 2007), no transactivation capacity was detected for TAΔp53α which lacks part of its DBD and linker region to its OD as well as the nuclear localization signal (NLS) and for the p53ψ isoform (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Δ40p53α and Δ40p53β showed a slight transactivation capacity (100- to 200-fold below wt-p53).
source: Δ40p53α and Δ40p53β showed a slight transactivation capacity (100- to 200-fold below wt-p53).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: The Δ133 and Δ160 N-terminal truncations showed no transcriptional activity at all, independent of their C-terminus.
source: The other N-terminal truncations (Δ133 and Δ160) showed no activity at all, independent of their C-terminus (α, β, and γ), consistent with a lack of the entire TAD and parts of the DBD as well as depending on the C-terminus a lack of the OD (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-C

claim: β-isoforms were much stronger expressed compared to α-isoforms.
source: The expression levels of the constructs differed with β-isoforms being much stronger expressed compared to α-isoforms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The γ-isoforms showed the lowest expression of all C-terminal truncations.
source: The γ-isoforms showed the lowest expression of all C-terminal truncations, while the lowest expression levels among the N-terminal isoforms were seen for the Δ133p53 isoforms.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The lowest expression levels among the N-terminal isoforms were seen for the Δ133p53 isoforms.
source: The γ-isoforms showed the lowest expression of all C-terminal truncations, while the lowest expression levels among the N-terminal isoforms were seen for the Δ133p53 isoforms.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Only wtp53 and Δ40p53α showed binding to the p53-REs in DNA pulldown assays.
source: Only wtp53 and Δ40p53α showed binding to the p53-REs (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: For high-affinity DNA binding, p53 family members need a folded DBD and the ability to form tetramers.
source: For high-affinity DNA binding, p53 family members need a folded DBD and the ability to form tetramers.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: For all other p53 isoforms except wtp53 and Δ40p53α, no DNA binding could be observed due to the lack of a folded DBD or lack of a functional OD or a combination of both.
source: For all other p53 isoforms, no DNA binding could be observed due to the lack of a folded DBD (Δ133, Δ160 constructs, and p53ψ), lack of a functional OD (β- and ɣ-C-termini) or a combination of both.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and logical inference

claim: The affinity of Δ40p53β for DNA was ~280-fold lower than the artificial DBD-OD construct and comparable to the affinity of the isolated p53 DBD.
source: The artificial DBD-OD construct showed high affinity, while the affinity for the Δ40p53β was ~280-fold lower and comparable to the affinity of the isolated p53 DBD (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by SPR experimental data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: All p53 isoforms except Δ40p53α show a behaviour more comparable to mutant p53 than to wtp53.
source: Summarizing the transactivation and DNA-binding assays, all p53 isoforms show a behaviour more comparable to mutant p53 than to wtp53.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data presented

claim: Δ40p53α is able to bind DNA without exhibiting a significant transcriptional activity.
source: Only Δ40p53α is able to bind DNA without exhibiting a significant transcriptional activity.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data presented

claim: The E6 protein binds to a region of the p53 DBD different from the DNA-binding interface.
source: The E6 protein binds to a region of the p53 DBD different from the DNA-binding interface (Figure 3A) and initiates the degradation of p53 by the ubiquitin proteasome system (Martinez-Zapien et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2024; Münick et al., 2025).
evidence: Supported by citations and shown in Figure 3A

claim: The E6 protein initiates the degradation of p53 by the ubiquitin proteasome system.
source: The E6 protein binds to a region of the p53 DBD different from the DNA-binding interface (Figure 3A) and initiates the degradation of p53 by the ubiquitin proteasome system (Martinez-Zapien et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2024; Münick et al., 2025).
evidence: Supported by citations to Martinez-Zapien et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2024; Münick et al., 2025

claim: An unfolded DBD or a DBD with a non-wild-type conformation does not get degraded by E6.
source: An unfolded DBD or a DBD with a non-wild-type conformation does not get degraded.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: wtp53 was completely degraded in the E6 degradation assay.
source: As expected, wtp53 was completely degraded in this assay (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The structural mutant V157F was not degraded at all in the E6 degradation assay.
source: Another structural mutant V157F was not degraded at all.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The R273H mutation that is located in the DNA-binding interface did not inhibit degradation by E6.
source: The R273H mutation that is located in the DNA-binding interface did not inhibit degradation, demonstrating that it retains the wild-type fold of the DBD.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: TAp53ψ and TAΔp53α showed no decreased signal in the presence of HPV E6.
source: TAp53ψ and TAΔp53α showed no decreased signal in the presence of HPV E6.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: TAp53ψ and TAΔp53α are not able to fold their DBD correctly.
source: Both lack C-terminal parts of the DBD, indicating that these isoforms are not able to fold their DBD correctly.
evidence: Inferred from the E6 degradation assay results

claim: TAp53β, TAp53ɣ, Δ40p53β and Δ40p53ɣ are degraded by E6, although not as efficiently as wtp53.
source: Isoforms that contain a complete DBD should be sensitive to this degradation assay and consequently, TAp53β, TAp53ɣ as well as Δ40p53β and Δ40p53ɣ are degraded, although not as efficiently as wtp53.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The Δ133p53 and Δ160p53 isoforms show only low levels or even no degradation by E6.
source: The remaining p53 isoforms with deletions in the DBD (Δ133p53α-γ and Δ160p53α-γ) show only low levels or even no degradation, similar to ΔNp63α which we have added as a negative control.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The pAB240 antibody binds an epitope in the DBD of p53, which is only exposed when the domain is unfolded.
source: The latter binds an epitope in the DBD of p53, which is only exposed when the domain is unfolded (Schmieg and Simmons, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schmieg and Simmons, 1993

claim: The two p53 mutants R175H and V157F were efficiently immunoprecipitated by the pAB240 antibody.
source: The results showed that the two p53 mutants R175H and V157F were efficiently immunoprecipitated (IP).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: All Δ133 and in particular all Δ160 isoforms as well as p53ψ and TAΔp53α interacted with the pAB240 antibody.
source: Likewise, all Δ133 and in particular all Δ160 isoforms as well as p53ψ and TAΔp53α interacted with this antibody.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The G4 DARPin pulled down wtp53 as well as the R273H mutant.
source: The G4 DARPin pulled down wtp53 as well as the R273H mutant.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and 3E

claim: The R175H mutant was pulled down by the G4 DARPin, albeit with a lower efficiency with H1299 cells expressed protein.
source: The R175H mutant was also pulled down, albeit with a lower efficiency with H1299 cells expressed protein (due to the higher temperature of cell culture compared to expression in rabbit reticulocyte lysate (RRL) which results in a lower level of the DBD with wild-type conformation).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and 3E

claim: The efficiency of G4 DARPin pulldown for the V157F mutant was very low.
source: The efficiency for the V157F mutant was very low.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and 3E

claim: None of the Δ133 isoforms or the p53ψ and TAΔp53α showed interaction with the G4 DARPin.
source: None of the Δ133 isoforms or the p53ψ and TAΔp53α showed interaction.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and 3E

claim: Only wtp53 and the Δ40p53 variants contain a fully folded DBD.
source: Together, these binding studies demonstrated that only wtp53 and the Δ40p53 variants contain a fully folded DBD.
evidence: Inferred from the E6 degradation, pAB240 binding, and DARPin pulldown experiments

claim: High-affinity DNA binding requires a functional OD which enables only wtp53 and Δ40p53α to interact strongly.
source: High-affinity DNA binding in addition requires a functional OD which enables only wtp53 and Δ40p53α to interact strongly.
evidence: Inferred from the DNA binding experiments and structural knowledge

claim: The DBD contains an aggregation-prone peptide sequence that is usually hidden within the folded structure but gets exposed upon unfolding.
source: The DBD contains an aggregation-prone peptide sequence that is usually hidden within the folded structure but gets exposed upon unfolding (Wang and Fersht, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang and Fersht, 2015

claim: Mutations within the SAM domain of p63 lead to the exposure of a usually hidden aggregation-prone peptide which results in aggregation of p63.
source: In the case of p63, we had previously shown that mutations within the SAM domain also led to the exposure of a usually hidden aggregation-prone peptide which results in aggregation of p63 (Russo et al., 2018) as the cause of the ankyloblepharon-ectodermal defects-cleft lip/palate (AEC) syndrome, in human patients (McGrath et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Russo et al., 2018 and McGrath et al., 2001

claim: Frame shift mutations in p63 cause the AEC syndrome by creating new aggregation-prone sequences.
source: In addition to point mutations in the SAM domain, frame shift mutations also cause the AEC syndrome by creating new aggregation-prone sequences (Russo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Russo et al., 2018

claim: The TANGO algorithm predicted the presence of novel APRs in the DBD of TAp53ψ and the OD of p53ɣ.
source: This analysis predicted indeed the presence of novel APRs in the DBD of TAp53ψ and the OD of p53ɣ (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Supported by in silico prediction shown in Figure 4A-C

claim: wtp53 and p53R273H showed a tetrameric state in analytical SEC.
source: The results indicated a tetrameric state for wtp53 as well as for p53R273H and Δ40p53α (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by analytical SEC data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Δ40p53α showed a tetrameric state in analytical SEC.
source: The results indicated a tetrameric state for wtp53 as well as for p53R273H and Δ40p53α (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by analytical SEC data shown in Figure 4D

claim: The cancer mutant p53R175H showed a mixture of tetrameric protein and partial aggregation in analytical SEC.
source: The cancer mutant p53R175H showed a mixture of tetrameric protein and partial aggregation indicated by a shift to higher molecular weight.
evidence: Supported by analytical SEC data shown in Figure 4D

claim: TAp53β and Δ40p53β showed a shift towards lower molecular weight in analytical SEC, consistent with their inability to form tetramers.
source: TAp53β and Δ40p53β showed a shift towards lower molecular weight, consistent with their inability to form tetramers, while TAp53ɣ and Δ40p53ɣ exhibited additional aggregation behaviour.
evidence: Supported by analytical SEC data shown in Figure 4D

claim: TAp53ɣ and Δ40p53ɣ exhibited aggregation behaviour in analytical SEC.
source: TAp53β and Δ40p53β showed a shift towards lower molecular weight, consistent with their inability to form tetramers, while TAp53ɣ and Δ40p53ɣ exhibited additional aggregation behaviour.
evidence: Supported by analytical SEC data shown in Figure 4D

claim: The Δ133 and Δ160 isoforms with β- and ɣ-C-termini displayed very strong aggregation in analytical SEC.
source: Of the Δ133 and Δ160 isoforms, the α-C-terminus showed only a slight aggregation tendency, while both β- and ɣ-C-termini displayed very strong aggregation, as did the TAp53Ψ and TAΔp53 isoforms.
evidence: Supported by analytical SEC data shown in Figure 4D

claim: TAp53Ψ and TAΔp53 isoforms displayed very strong aggregation in analytical SEC.
source: Of the Δ133 and Δ160 isoforms, the α-C-terminus showed only a slight aggregation tendency, while both β- and ɣ-C-termini displayed very strong aggregation, as did the TAp53Ψ and TAΔp53 isoforms.
evidence: Supported by analytical SEC data shown in Figure 4D

claim: All Δ133 and Δ160 isoforms showed strong aggregation in native PAGE.
source: We further investigated the behaviour of these isoforms (aggregation is independent of Myc-tag position; Figure 4—figure supplement 1) by native PAGE with similar results, except that in this experimental setting also the Δ133p53α and Δ160p53α isoforms showed strong aggregation (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by native PAGE data shown in Figure 4E

claim: All Δ133 and Δ160 isoforms were found to a large degree in the insoluble fraction after expression in H1299 cells.
source: Finally, we determined the relative amounts of protein in the soluble and insoluble fraction after expression in H1299 cells. In this assay, again all Δ133 and Δ160 isoforms were found to a large degree in the insoluble fraction (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by solubility assay data shown in Figure 4F

claim: Δ40p53ɣ was mainly found in the pellet (insoluble fraction) in solubility assays.
source: Δ40p53ɣ was also mainly found in the pellet while TAp53ɣ was mainly soluble as were the TAp53ψ and TAΔp53 isoforms.
evidence: Supported by solubility assay data shown in Figure 4F

claim: TAp53ɣ was mainly soluble in solubility assays.
source: Δ40p53ɣ was also mainly found in the pellet while TAp53ɣ was mainly soluble as were the TAp53ψ and TAΔp53 isoforms.
evidence: Supported by solubility assay data shown in Figure 4F

claim: TAp53ψ and TAΔp53 isoforms were mainly soluble in solubility assays.
source: Δ40p53ɣ was also mainly found in the pellet while TAp53ɣ was mainly soluble as were the TAp53ψ and TAΔp53 isoforms.
evidence: Supported by solubility assay data shown in Figure 4F

claim: Thioflavin T binding was confirmed for the ɣ-peptide.
source: Thioflavin T binding was confirmed for the ɣ-peptide, while the β-peptide did not show binding above the background level, suggesting that indeed the ɣ-C-terminus has a high aggregation propensity in vitro and in cellulo (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by ThT fluorescence assay data shown in Figure 4G

claim: The β-peptide did not show Thioflavin T binding above the background level.
source: Thioflavin T binding was confirmed for the ɣ-peptide, while the β-peptide did not show binding above the background level, suggesting that indeed the ɣ-C-terminus has a high aggregation propensity in vitro and in cellulo (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by ThT fluorescence assay data shown in Figure 4G

claim: The ɣ-C-terminus has a high aggregation propensity in vitro and in cellulo.
source: Thioflavin T binding was confirmed for the ɣ-peptide, while the β-peptide did not show binding above the background level, suggesting that indeed the ɣ-C-terminus has a high aggregation propensity in vitro and in cellulo (Figure 4G).
evidence: Inferred from ThT fluorescence assay data shown in Figure 4G

claim: Δ133p53α,β could be kept soluble when expressed under a minimal CMV promoter which results in reduced expression levels.
source: To test the dependence on the concentration, we expressed several isoforms under a minimal CMV promoter (selected artificial promoter, p5RPU.Myc [Brown et al., 2017], was cloned into pcDNA3.1 plasmid) which results in reduced expression levels in H1299 cells. Using this system, also Δ133p53α,β could indeed be kept soluble (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), suggesting that aggregation will only become a problem if the expression level surpasses a certain threshold level.
evidence: Supported by solubility assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: Aggregation of p53 isoforms will only become a problem if the expression level surpasses a certain threshold level.
source: Using this system, also Δ133p53α,β could indeed be kept soluble (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), suggesting that aggregation will only become a problem if the expression level surpasses a certain threshold level.
evidence: Inferred from solubility assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: For both Δ133p53α and Δ133p53β, the percentage of the insoluble fraction increased relative to the treatment with only DMSO when treated with HSP70 and HSP90 inhibitors.
source: For both Δ133p53α and Δ133p53β, however, the percentage of the insoluble fraction increased relative to the treatment with only DMSO, suggesting that inhibition of chaperones results in increased aggregation (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by solubility assay data with chaperone inhibitors shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: Inhibition of chaperones results in increased aggregation of Δ133p53α and Δ133p53β.
source: For both Δ133p53α and Δ133p53β, however, the percentage of the insoluble fraction increased relative to the treatment with only DMSO, suggesting that inhibition of chaperones results in increased aggregation (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Inferred from solubility assay data with chaperone inhibitors shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: A strong signal for HSC/HSP70 co-immunoprecipitation was detected for the cancer mutant p53V157F.
source: A strong signal was detected for the cancer mutant p53V157F (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Interactions with HSC/HSP70 were seen for Δ40p53ɣ, Δ133α,β,ɣ, TAp53ψ, and TAΔp53.
source: Further interactions were seen for Δ40p53ɣ, Δ133α,β,ɣ, TAp53ψ, and TAΔp53.
evidence: Supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Only weak signals for HSC/HSP70 co-immunoprecipitation occurred for wtp53, Δ40p53α, Δ40p53β, and p53R273H.
source: Only weak signals occurred for wtp53, Δ40p53α, Δ40p53β, and p53R273H in agreement with the interpretation that these isoforms and mutants do not have accessible hydrophobic patches or APRs.
evidence: Supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Expression of p53 isoforms containing a ɣ-C-terminus led to a strong activation of the HSP70 promoter.
source: These experiments showed that expression of p53 isoforms containing a ɣ-C-terminus, as well as all Δ133p53 versions, led to a strong activation of the HSP70 promoter.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Expression of all Δ133p53 versions led to a strong activation of the HSP70 promoter.
source: These experiments showed that expression of p53 isoforms containing a ɣ-C-terminus, as well as all Δ133p53 versions, led to a strong activation of the HSP70 promoter.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Elevated levels of HSP70 promoter activation were detected for TAΔp53, p53R175H, and p53V157F.
source: Elevated levels were also detected for TAΔp53, p53R175H, and p53V157F, but not for the DNA-binding interface mutant p53R273H.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The ɣ-C-terminus strongly induced activity on the HSP70 promoter when fused to Scarlet.
source: The results showed that the ɣ-C-terminus strongly induced activity, but not the β-C-terminus.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The β-C-terminus did not induce activity on the HSP70 promoter when fused to Scarlet.
source: The results showed that the ɣ-C-terminus strongly induced activity, but not the β-C-terminus.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The Y327A, L330A, L334A, and L336A mutations in the ɣ-C-terminus reduced the luciferase expression to background levels.
source: To investigate this hypothesis, we created the Y327A, L330A, L334A, and L336A mutations in the ɣ-C-terminus which indeed reduced the luciferase expression to background levels.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Luciferase expression via the HSP70 promoter was induced by the overexpression of certain p53 isoforms, suggesting that their only partially folded state and/or open hydrophobic patches induce a cellular stress response.
source: Overall, these results suggest that luciferase expression via the HSP70 promoter was induced by the overexpression of certain p53 isoforms, suggesting that their only partially folded state and/or open hydrophobic patches induce a cellular stress response.
evidence: Inferred from luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5B

claim: All p53 isoforms tested interact with a common set of proteins involved in chaperone function and binding to un- or misfolded proteins.
source: Figure 5D shows that all isoforms interact with a common set of proteins (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Δ133α, Δ133β, and TAp53ɣ showed close proximity to many more proteins involved in binding to un- or misfolded proteins compared to TAp53β and Δ40p53α.
source: In addition to this common set, TAp53β and Δ40p53α showed only very few additional interaction partners. This situation was very different for Δ133α, Δ133β, and TAp53ɣ, which all showed close proximity to many more proteins involved in binding to un- or misfolded proteins.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Δ133p53α can form mixed tetramers with wild-type p53.
source: For Δ133p53α, we could quantify a peptide precursor between amino acids 102 and 110 that is highly likely to originate from wild-type p53. This result is not surprising as Δ133p53α contains a full oligomerization domain capable of forming mixed tetramers with wild-type p53.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5E-G and logical inference

claim: Δ133p53β cannot hetero-oligomerize with wild-type p53.
source: These peptides were absent or beyond the detection limit in the Δ133p53β sample, in line with the interpretation that this isoform cannot hetero-oligomerize with wild-type p53.
evidence: Inferred from mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5E-G

claim: Δ133p53β, TAp53β, and TAp53ɣ do not interact with wild-type p53 via oligomerization.
source: For Δ133p53β, TAp53β, and TAp53ɣ, we did not find any peptides in this region (with the exception of a precursor of very low intensity in a single Δ133p53β sample), supporting the interpretation that these isoforms do not interact with wild-type p53.
evidence: Inferred from mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5E-G

claim: Δ133p53α can act dominantly negative towards wild-type p53 by forming mixed tetramers.
source: Overall, these data show that Δ133p53α can form mixed tetramers and can thus act dominantly negative towards wild-type p53.
evidence: Inferred from mass spectrometry data and functional assays

claim: Co-expression of known cancer mutants strongly inhibited the activity of wtp53.
source: Co-expression of known cancer mutants strongly inhibited the activity of wtp53 as expected, as did co-expression of all α-isoforms (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Co-expression of all α-isoforms strongly inhibited the activity of wtp53.
source: Co-expression of known cancer mutants strongly inhibited the activity of wtp53 as expected, as did co-expression of all α-isoforms (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Expression of the Δ40p53α isoform can inhibit the activity of wtp53 by blocking DNA binding (promoter squelching).
source: Expression of the Δ40p53α isoform can inhibit the activity of wtp53 also by blocking DNA binding (promoter squelching).
evidence: Inferred from luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Co-expression of any isoform that is incapable of forming tetramers did not show any inhibitory effect on wtp53.
source: Co-expression of any isoform that is incapable of forming tetramers did not show any inhibitory effect.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6A

claim: TAΔp53α is trapped in the cytoplasm due to lack of NLS, preventing a dominant negative effect on wtp53.
source: However, the deleted sequence includes the NLS of the protein, which traps this isoform in the cytoplasm and prevents a dominant negative effect as also previously described (Chan and Poon, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chan and Poon, 2007 and logical inference

claim: Co-expression with Δ40p53α strongly inhibited the activity of TAp73α.
source: Co-expression with Δ40p53α again strongly inhibited the activity of TAp73α, not through formation of mixed tetramers but by promoter squelching which could be confirmed from the inability of a R273H mutant of Δ40p53α to inhibit p73.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Δ40p53α inhibits TAp73α by promoter squelching, not through formation of mixed tetramers.
source: Co-expression with Δ40p53α again strongly inhibited the activity of TAp73α, not through formation of mixed tetramers but by promoter squelching which could be confirmed from the inability of a R273H mutant of Δ40p53α to inhibit p73.
evidence: Inferred from luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The Δ133 isoforms showed an intermediate degree of inhibition of TAp73α activity.
source: All other p53 isoforms tested had no effect, consistent with their inability to bind to DNA and replace p73. The only exceptions were the Δ133 isoforms that showed an intermediate degree of inhibition.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The inhibitory effect of the Δ133p53 isoforms on TAp73β was strongly reduced compared to TAp73α.
source: The results mirror the data obtained with TAp73α, with the exception that the inhibitory effect of the Δ133p53 isoforms was indeed strongly reduced (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6C

claim: The α-C-termini of p73α and p63α can confer co-aggregation with destabilized p53 cancer mutants such as p53R175H.
source: In a previous study, we had shown that the α-C-termini of p73α and p63α can confer co-aggregation with destabilized p53 cancer mutants such as p53R175H (Kehrloesser et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kehrloesser et al., 2016

claim: Δ40p53α interacted strongly with wtp53 as well as with the p53R175H and p53R273H cancer mutants in co-IP experiments.
source: Δ40p53α interacted strongly with wtp53 as well as with the p53R175H and p53R273H cancer mutants, while Δ40p53β interacted weakly only with p53R175H, suggesting that these interactions are mediated by the OD.
evidence: Supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 6F

claim: Δ40p53β interacted weakly only with p53R175H in co-IP experiments.
source: Δ40p53α interacted strongly with wtp53 as well as with the p53R175H and p53R273H cancer mutants, while Δ40p53β interacted weakly only with p53R175H, suggesting that these interactions are mediated by the OD.
evidence: Supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 6F

claim: Interaction of Δ133p53α with all three p53 variants resulted in co-IPs.
source: Similarly, interaction with all three p53 variants resulted in co-IPs with Δ133p53α.
evidence: Supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 6F

claim: Δ133p53α can drag wtp53 into insoluble aggregates, but not very efficiently.
source: Interaction with wtp53 was weakest, showing that Δ133p53α can drag wtp53 into insoluble aggregates, but not very efficiently.
evidence: Inferred from co-IP data shown in Figure 6F

claim: The strongest co-IP of Δ133p53β was with the p53R175H cancer mutant which forms co-aggregates.
source: Of the Δ133p53β co-IPs, the strongest was with the p53R175H cancer mutant which forms co-aggregates.
evidence: Supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 6F

claim: None of the p63 isoforms tested (TAp63α, ΔNp63α, ΔNp63αV603D) showed interaction with Δ40p53α or Δ40p53β in co-IP experiments.
source: For p63, we tested the dimeric TAp63α, the open tetrameric ΔNp63α and the ΔNp63αV603D version in which the aggregation-prone C-terminus is mutated to reduce the aggregation propensity (Kehrloesser et al., 2016). None of them showed interaction with Δ40p53α or Δ40p53β.
evidence: Supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 6F

claim: A co-IP could be detected for ΔNp63α and Δ133p53β, which could be reduced by the V603D mutation in the p63 C-terminus.
source: A co-IP could, however, be detected for ΔNp63α and Δ133p53β, which could be reduced by the V603D mutation in the p63 C-terminus, showing that this interaction is based on co-aggregation.
evidence: Supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 6F

claim: The interaction between ΔNp63α and Δ133p53β is based on co-aggregation.
source: A co-IP could, however, be detected for ΔNp63α and Δ133p53β, which could be reduced by the V603D mutation in the p63 C-terminus, showing that this interaction is based on co-aggregation.
evidence: Inferred from co-IP data shown in Figure 6F

claim: TAp73α shows co-aggregation with Δ133p53α and Δ133p53β, which can be reduced by a V586D mutation in the α-C-terminus.
source: TAp73α, which is a constitutively open and tetrameric isoform (Luh et al., 2013), shows co-aggregation with Δ133p53α and Δ133p53β, which can get reduced by a V586D mutation in the α-C-terminus that reduces the aggregation propensity (Kehrloesser et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 6F and citations

claim: TAp73β, which lacks the α-C-terminus, shows a strongly reduced co-IP with Δ133p53 isoforms.
source: Likewise, TAp73β, which lacks the α-C-terminus, shows a strongly reduced co-IP.
evidence: Supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 6F

claim: ΔNp63α plays an important role in organizing the chromatin landscape in the basal cells of epithelial tissues.
source: In the case of p63, very clear biological functions have been assigned to two of these, namely ΔNp63α which plays an important role in organizing the chromatin landscape in the basal cells of epithelial tissues (Yang et al., 1998; Kouwenhoven et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Yang et al., 1998 and Kouwenhoven et al., 2015

claim: TAp63α is a crucial factor for maintaining the genetic quality in oocytes.
source: and TAp63α which is a crucial factor for maintaining the genetic quality in oocytes (Deutsch et al., 2011; Suh et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Deutsch et al., 2011 and Suh et al., 2006

claim: For p73, functions in the development and maintenance of neurons, the development of ciliated cells and in tumour suppression have been described.
source: For p73 functions in the development and maintenance of neurons, the development of ciliated cells (Marshall et al., 2016) and in tumour suppression (Logotheti et al., 2022) has been described involving both TA- and ΔN-isoforms with the α- and the β-C-termini.
evidence: Supported by citations to Marshall et al., 2016 and Logotheti et al., 2022

claim: With the exception of Δ40p53α, all p53 isoforms are characterized by containing only parts of the DBD and/or the OD.
source: With the exception of Δ40p53α, which lacks parts of the unstructured transactivation domain, all are characterized by containing only parts of the DBD and/or the OD.
evidence: Stated as a fact in the manuscript text

claim: Protein folding of single domains is in general a cooperative process.
source: As protein folding of single domains is in general a cooperative process, this predicts that these domains with missing secondary structure elements are largely unfolded and not capable of fulfilling a normal cellular function.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: Domains with missing secondary structure elements are largely unfolded and not capable of fulfilling a normal cellular function.
source: As protein folding of single domains is in general a cooperative process, this predicts that these domains with missing secondary structure elements are largely unfolded and not capable of fulfilling a normal cellular function.
evidence: Inferred from protein folding principles

claim: High-affinity DNA binding requires both a folded DBD as well as a folded OD.
source: Our data demonstrate that high-affinity DNA binding requires both a folded DBD as well as a folded OD.
evidence: Demonstrated by the experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Only Δ40p53α fulfils the requirements for high-affinity DNA binding and might have its own meaningful biological function.
source: Only Δ40p53α fulfils these requirements and might have its own meaningful biological function, potentially as a transcriptional inhibitor of wtp53, similar to ΔNp63 and ΔNp73 isoforms which can inhibit wtp53 by promoter squelching.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data and comparison to p63/p73 isoforms

claim: The potential role of Δ40p53α could be that of fine tuning of wtp53's activity.
source: The potential role of Δ40p53α could be that of fine tuning of wtp53's activity as the formation of hetero-complexes with a reduced number of TADs influences not only the transcriptional activity directly but potentially also indirectly as a reduced number of TADs can reduce the Mdm2-dependent degradation rate.
evidence: Stated as speculation by the authors

claim: All other p53 isoforms do not bind strongly to DNA either due to lack of a functional DBD, a functional OD or even both.
source: All other p53 isoforms do not bind strongly to DNA either due to lack of a functional DBD, a functional OD or even both.
evidence: Demonstrated by the experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: The unfolded/partial folded states of p53 isoforms increase cellular stress as evidenced by the upregulation of chaperones.
source: Instead, the unfolded/partial folded states, in particular of the DBD, as well as the hydrophobic nature of the ɣ-C-terminus, increase cellular stress as evidenced by the upregulation of chaperones and the association of chaperones and proteins involved in interaction with unfolded/misfolded proteins with these isoforms.
evidence: Demonstrated by the experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Below a certain expression level, the cellular chaperone systems are able to keep p53 isoforms soluble.
source: Below a certain expression level, the cellular chaperone systems seem to be able to keep these isoforms soluble, but above this level they accumulate in insoluble aggregates.
evidence: Demonstrated by the experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Above a certain expression level, p53 isoforms accumulate in insoluble aggregates.
source: Below a certain expression level, the cellular chaperone systems seem to be able to keep these isoforms soluble, but above this level they accumulate in insoluble aggregates.
evidence: Demonstrated by the experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: p53 isoforms have the potential to inactivate members of the p53 protein family by forming inactive hetero-complexes with wtp53 (Δ133p53α and Δ160p53α).
source: While the lack of crucial functional domains prevents well-defined physiological roles of these isoforms (with the potential exception of Δ40p53α as mentioned above), they have the potential to inactivate members of the p53 protein family by forming inactive hetero-complexes with wtp53 (Δ133p53α and Δ160p53α), by direct co-aggregation with α-isoforms of p63 and p73 (Δ133p53α,β,ɣ and Δ160p53α,β,ɣ) or promoter squelching (Δ40p53α).
evidence: Demonstrated by the experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: p53 isoforms have the potential to inactivate members of the p53 protein family by direct co-aggregation with α-isoforms of p63 and p73 (Δ133p53α,β,ɣ and Δ160p53α,β,ɣ).
source: While the lack of crucial functional domains prevents well-defined physiological roles of these isoforms (with the potential exception of Δ40p53α as mentioned above), they have the potential to inactivate members of the p53 protein family by forming inactive hetero-complexes with wtp53 (Δ133p53α and Δ160p53α), by direct co-aggregation with α-isoforms of p63 and p73 (Δ133p53α,β,ɣ and Δ160p53α,β,ɣ) or promoter squelching (Δ40p53α).
evidence: Demonstrated by the experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: p53 isoforms have the potential to inactivate members of the p53 protein family by promoter squelching (Δ40p53α).
source: While the lack of crucial functional domains prevents well-defined physiological roles of these isoforms (with the potential exception of Δ40p53α as mentioned above), they have the potential to inactivate members of the p53 protein family by forming inactive hetero-complexes with wtp53 (Δ133p53α and Δ160p53α), by direct co-aggregation with α-isoforms of p63 and p73 (Δ133p53α,β,ɣ and Δ160p53α,β,ɣ) or promoter squelching (Δ40p53α).
evidence: Demonstrated by the experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: TAΔp53α aggregates.
source: The exception to this rule is TAΔp53α, which aggregates (García-Alai et al., 2008) and could in theory bind to wtp53 via its OD, but lacks an NLS and therefore cannot be imported into the nucleus to execute its dominant negative effect.
evidence: Supported by citation to García-Alai et al., 2008

claim: Forced translocation of TAΔp53α into the nucleus establishes a dominant negative effect.
source: Forced translocation of TAΔp53α into the nucleus was shown to establish a dominant negative effect, demonstrating that the lack of the NLS is the main impairment of a negative effect on wtp53 (Chan and Poon, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chan and Poon, 2007

claim: Through various mechanisms, expression of many of the p53 isoforms can have detrimental effects.
source: Through these mechanisms, expression of many of the p53 isoforms can have detrimental effects, and the literature on these isoforms so far shows a clear correlation with cancer.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data and literature

claim: The literature on p53 isoforms shows a clear correlation with cancer.
source: Through these mechanisms, expression of many of the p53 isoforms can have detrimental effects, and the literature on these isoforms so far shows a clear correlation with cancer.
evidence: Stated as a summary of the literature

claim: The least effect is to be expected from Δ40p53β.
source: The least effect is to be expected from Δ40p53β, which is only little more than an isolated p53 DBD and Δ40p53ɣ.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data presented

claim: Δ40p53ɣ has the ability to aggregate and co-aggregate with other proteins due to the very hydrophobic nature of the ɣ-C-terminus.
source: This isoform, however, has the ability to aggregate and co-aggregate with other proteins due to the very hydrophobic nature of the ɣ-C-terminus.
evidence: Demonstrated by the experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: For all other p53 isoforms except Δ40p53β and Δ40p53ɣ, severe effects – increasing with the cellular concentration – can be expected.
source: For all other isoforms, severe effects – increasing with the cellular concentration – can be expected.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data presented

claim: Deletion of the unfolded N-terminal as well as C-terminal domains also impairs the normal function of p53.
source: While this study is focused on the effects that truncations have on the folded domains of p53, it should be mentioned that deletion of the unfolded N-terminal as well as C-terminal domains also impairs the normal function of p53 (Dyson and Wright, 2025).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dyson and Wright, 2025

claim: The unfolded N-terminal and C-terminal domains of p53 are the target of a large number of post-translational modifications and are important for the interaction with regulatory proteins.
source: These domains are the target of a large number of post-translational modifications and are important for the interaction with regulatory proteins, for example p300 and Mdm2 in the transactivation domain.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: Δ133p53α interacts with members of the Hsp70 chaperone families as well as the chaperone-associated E3 ubiquitin ligase STUB1 as well as BAG2 and BAG5.
source: The lab of Curtis Harris has shown by mass spectrometry analysis following co-IP of FLAG-tagged Δ133p53α in MRC-5 fibroblasts that Δ133p53α interacts with members of the Hsp70 chaperone families as well as the chaperone-associated E3 ubiquitin ligase STUB1 as well as BAG2 and BAG5 (Horikawa et al., 2014), similar to our Turbo-ID-based proteomics study reported here (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by citation to Horikawa et al., 2014

claim: A computational study of the Δ133p53 DBD suggested a lower stability correlated with a high tendency for aggregation.
source: whereas a computational study of the Δ133p53 DBD suggested a lower stability correlated with a high tendency for aggregation (Lei et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lei et al., 2019

claim: Δ133p53β interacts with the CCT chaperone complex and depletion of this complex further promotes aggregation.
source: Experimentally, the aggregation behaviour of Δ133p53β has been investigated by Arsic et al., 2021. They also found that this isoform interacts with the CCT chaperone complex and that depletion of this complex further promotes aggregation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Arsic et al., 2021

claim: The TAΔp53 isoform cannot bind to the p21 promoter.
source: Direct experimental evidence for the instability and aggregation tendency of the TAΔp53 isoform was provided by the Fersht laboratory (García-Alai et al., 2008). They confirmed that this isoform cannot bind to the p21 promoter and in mixed states significantly reduces the DNA-binding affinity of wtp53.
evidence: Supported by citation to García-Alai et al., 2008

claim: In mixed states, TAΔp53 significantly reduces the DNA-binding affinity of wtp53.
source: Direct experimental evidence for the instability and aggregation tendency of the TAΔp53 isoform was provided by the Fersht laboratory (García-Alai et al., 2008). They confirmed that this isoform cannot bind to the p21 promoter and in mixed states significantly reduces the DNA-binding affinity of wtp53.
evidence: Supported by citation to García-Alai et al., 2008

claim: Numerous studies have shown that the only metastable DBD of p53 gets further destabilized by structural mutations leading to loss of DNA binding and aggregation behaviour.
source: All the data suggesting that deletion of parts of the DBD results in the inability to bind DNA, the exposure of aggregation-prone peptide sequences and aggregation as well as co-aggregation with other cellular factors are supported by a large literature on the effect of structural mutations in the p53 DBD. Numerous studies have shown that the only metastable DBD of p53 gets further destabilized by these mutations leading to loss of DNA binding and aggregation behaviour (Xu et al., 2011; Wang and Fersht, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Xu et al., 2011 and Wang and Fersht, 2015

claim: If single point mutations in the DBD can have strong effects, deletions of entire parts of the domain will have even stronger effects.
source: If single point mutations in the DBD can have that strong effects, it is more than likely that deletions of entire parts of the domain will have even stronger effects – consistent with all the data reported here.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of mutation effects to deletion effects

claim: The effects seen in cell culture as well as in patients with overexpression of different p53 isoforms should be interpreted on the background of the aggregation propensity as well as a potential overload of the cellular chaperone system.
source: In conclusion, the effects seen in cell culture as well as in patients with overexpression of different p53 isoforms should be interpreted on the background of the aggregation propensity as well as a potential overload of the cellular chaperone system instead of any specific interaction of these isoforms with proteins or DNA.
evidence: Stated as the authors' conclusion based on all the data presented
